| NC | [Charles Leclerc](/drivers/charles-leclerc) | [Ferrari](/teams/ferrari) | DNF, lap 2 | |

## Ferrari lost their home race in two laps

[Charles Leclerc](/drivers/charles-leclerc) started third and [Lewis Hamilton](/drivers/lewis-hamilton) fourth, both on softs, both aiming for the same piece of road. Hamilton went down the inside into the first chicane, Leclerc held his line, they touched, and Hamilton was in the gravel and [down to ninth](https://www.formula1.com/en/video/2026-Italian-Grand-Prix-Gasly-leads-away-as-Hamilton-drops-to-p9-on-the-race-start.1875588277934901342) before the lap was out. "Charles pushed me off," he said on the radio. No penalty followed, and the FIA published no decision document about it at all.

Then it got worse. At the end of lap two, defending fourth from [Oscar Piastri](/drivers/oscar-piastri), Leclerc got a snap of oversteer on the exit of the Parabolica and went into the outside barrier hard. He climbed out unhurt. The safety car became a red flag because the barrier needed rebuilding, and the race stopped for about half an hour.

Leclerc suggested afterwards there may have been a throttle issue, and [Ferrari](/teams/ferrari) went away to look at whether a torque spike was involved. It looked uncomfortably like his 2020 crash at the same corner.

## Hamilton wants it in writing

The fallout was the more interesting half. Hamilton said afterwards that [Ferrari have "no rules"](https://www.skysports.com/f1/news/12433/13582222/lewis-hamilton-claims-there-are-no-rules-at-ferrari-after-clash-with-team-mate-charles-leclerc-during-italian-gp) governing how their drivers race each other, that at [Mercedes](/teams/mercedes) the rules of engagement were written down, and that this needs sorting. He maintained he was ahead at the apex of Turn 2. Leclerc said the two of them had gone too far and took some of it on himself, and Hamilton declined the shared blame.

![Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari on track at Monza](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Lewis_Hamilton_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg/1280px-Lewis_Hamilton_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg)

*Hamilton at Monza in 2025, his first season in the Ferrari. Eustace Bagge, [CC BY 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lewis_Hamilton_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg), via Wikimedia Commons.*

Our view: Hamilton is right that Ferrari should have written rules, and wrong that this incident is the argument for them. He attacked a team-mate on the opening lap at the one circuit where the car behind always has a run, and got the outcome that move usually gets. What the weekend actually exposed is that Ferrari now have two drivers who will not yield to each other and no agreed answer for what happens next. That is a problem for Madrid, not a problem for Monza.

## The nineteenth-place win

[Mercedes](/teams/mercedes) chose this. Antonelli needed a full new power unit at some point in the season, they ran the numbers at Zandvoort, and the numbers said Monza. Toto Wolff put it about as bluntly as a team principal can: the calculations picked the track, and algorithms do not take a driver's nationality into account.

He took seven places on the opening lap, nineteenth to twelfth, before Leclerc's crash stopped the race. He restarted twelfth and was eighth by the end of the first racing lap. Then past [Oscar Piastri](/drivers/oscar-piastri), past Hamilton, past [Max Verstappen](/drivers/max-verstappen), and past [George Russell](/drivers/george-russell) into the first chicane on lap 18 for the lead.

A mid-race virtual safety car took it off him again. [Mercedes](/teams/mercedes) split their cars: Antonelli came in for fresh mediums and Russell stayed out on used hards, which handed his team-mate's track position back and then faded. Antonelli caught him, and on lap 49 of 53, attacking at the Variante del Rettifilo, went through the gravel and kept the car. Three laps from the flag he tried again and that one stuck.

He set the fastest lap of the race on the way to the flag, a 1:23.504 on lap 53, the last lap of the afternoon.

Two Mercedes trading the lead of a Grand Prix for thirty laps is either a thrilling advertisement for letting drivers race or a fortnight of awkward meetings, depending on how the season finishes. At Zandvoort the same team moved Russell aside for three points. At Monza they let it run, and the one who came through the field won it.

"This is a day that I will remember forever," Antonelli said. "It is for sure the most special win of my career so far." Russell, who led much of it and lost it twice, was shorter: "It's frustrating to be so close to victory and not to achieve it but that is racing sometimes." Toto Wolff called it "a phenomenal race by the team and both drivers".

## Gasly led, and Monza took it back

[Pierre Gasly](/drivers/pierre-gasly) had the pole, the launch and the lead, and finished seventh. That is not a failure, it is a description of the circuit. A low-drag [Alpine](/teams/alpine) that can qualify at the front is still an Alpine on lap thirty with a Mercedes in its mirrors, and Monza gives the car behind a tow the car in front cannot do anything about.

He led the opening laps of a Grand Prix at the circuit where he won one, six years after the fact. It was a good weekend, it deserved better than seventh, and seventh was always what it was going to be.

## Behind the podium

[Lando Norris](/drivers/lando-norris) took fourth off Piastri late on once his hard tyres came in, the two of them wheel-to-wheel with Norris briefly on the grass before [McLaren](/teams/mclaren) called it off. Their gap at the flag was 0.197s after 53 laps of Monza, and they are team-mates, which is the kind of thing that makes a pit wall reach for the radio.

![Lando Norris's McLaren on track at Monza](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Lando_Norris_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg/1280px-Lando_Norris_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg)

*Norris at Monza in 2025. Eustace Bagge, [CC BY 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lando_Norris_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg), via Wikimedia Commons.*

Fifteen cars finished on the lead lap and three retired. [Arvid Lindblad](/drivers/arvid-lindblad) was eighth and [Franco Colapinto](/drivers/franco-colapinto) ninth. [Fernando Alonso](/drivers/fernando-alonso) retired with suspected damage and [Lance Stroll](/drivers/lance-stroll) with hydraulics, so [Aston Martin](/teams/aston-martin) scored nothing and finished neither car. Alonso had started from the pit lane, as had [Liam Lawson](/drivers/liam-lawson), both for work done on the cars under parc ferme; only twenty of the twenty-two took the start from a grid slot at all.

## One result that is not final

Yuki Tsunoda finished tenth and was summoned afterwards. On the restart he approached the grid heading for the wrong box, corrected himself, and parked correctly; the race director ordered an extra formation lap anyway because, in his own evidence, he was not comfortable starting with the car in that position. Article B5.9.4 says a driver who causes an extra formation lap must then start from the pit lane, and Tsunoda did not.

The stewards took no further action, and their reasoning turns on something small. The penalty, they wrote, "is for failing to come into the Pit Lane and start from there. The penalty is not for causing the extra formation lap." To comply, a driver would have to know he was the cause, and nobody told [Racing Bulls](/teams/racing-bulls) he was.

[Audi](/teams/audi) have lodged a notice of intention to appeal, which is not the same as appealing. That notice buys 96 hours to decide whether to actually file. If they file and win, an unserved stop-and-go converts to a thirty-second penalty, Tsunoda drops to fifteenth, and [Gabriel Bortoleto](/drivers/gabriel-bortoleto) inherits the final point.

We are flagging it for a reason. Three days ago the FIA's International Court of Appeal reinstated Pierre Gasly's Monaco penalties and moved five drivers in a race run in June, and our own Monaco page needed correcting to match. A classification is not final until the appeals are.

## What it did to the championship

Antonelli leaves Monza on 267. Russell is second on 201, Hamilton third on 191, Norris fourth on 171 and Leclerc fifth on 155. The lead goes from 59 points to 66, and Antonelli now has seven of the thirteen wins this season to Russell's two, Norris' two, Hamilton's one and Leclerc's one.

The championship is now a Mercedes internal matter with Hamilton as the outside interest, and the awkward part for [Ferrari](/teams/ferrari) is that their two drivers spent Sunday racing each other into a barrier and a gravel trap while the title went past.

## Where it leaves us

**For the books:** the first Italian winner at Monza since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966, a win from nineteenth on the grid, Antonelli's seventh victory of the season, Gasly's first pole and the opening laps in his hands, Leclerc into the Parabolica barrier on lap two, a red flag and a thirty-minute stoppage, a Ferrari first-lap collision the stewards let stand, and a tenth place still under appeal.

The full classification is on the [race page](/series/f1/weekend/13/race), qualifying is on the [Qualifying page](/series/f1/weekend/13/qualifying), the whole weekend including the declared upgrades is on the [Italian Grand Prix hub](/series/f1/weekend/13), and the running totals are on the [standings](/series/f1/standings). [Formula 1's own report is here](https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/article/antonelli-beats-russell-to-italian-grand-prix-win-with-stunning-comeback-drive.15WtFEBT5JEe4drdeO88t2), and [the FIA's is here](https://www.fia.com/news/f1-antonelli-storms-19th-grid-take-sensational-home-win-monza-ahead-russell-and-verstappen).

Monza spent the whole weekend being told this was Ferrari's year to have a moment at home, with the engine step and the Schumacher anniversaries and both cars in the top six of every practice session. It got an Italian win instead, in a silver car, from nineteenth on the grid, by a driver who was not supposed to be anywhere near the front. The tifosi took it. They were never going to do anything else.

Madrid next, on a circuit nobody has raced.

*Cover photo: Antonelli at Monza in 2025. Eustace Bagge, [CC BY 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Andrea_Kimi_Antonelli_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying3.jpg), via Wikimedia Commons.*

title: F1 Italian GP 2026: Weekend Analysis - Friday lied about qualifying and told the truth about the race
summary: Second practice at Monza put George Russell first and Pierre Gasly fourteenth, and then Gasly took pole. Ignore the headline times, dig out the race runs hiding in the same session, and Friday afternoon had Sunday close to right, with one large hole where most of the podium should have been.
body:
[Second practice](/series/f1/weekend/13/practice-2) at Monza ended with [George Russell](/drivers/george-russell) fastest, [Charles Leclerc](/drivers/charles-leclerc) second and [Kimi Antonelli](/drivers/kimi-antonelli) third. [Pierre Gasly](/drivers/pierre-gasly) was fourteenth. Twenty-four hours later Gasly took [pole position](/series/f1/weekend/13/qualifying), which tells you what that classification was worth as a guide to Saturday.

Now ask it about Sunday instead. The driver with the best race pace in that session won the [Grand Prix](/series/f1/weekend/13/race) from nineteenth on the grid. The third best finished second. Gasly, eighth of the sixteen race runs completed all afternoon, finished seventh.

None of that is visible on the timing sheet. It is underneath it, in the laps nobody quotes.

## What a race run is, and how we dug them out

A Friday afternoon is two jobs sharing one car. The first is the low-fuel run that produces the headline time and the television graphic. The second is the race simulation: a long stint on one set of tyres, with fuel in the car, run at something close to the pace the driver expects to hold on Sunday. It is the only part of [the weekend](/information/formula-1/how-a-formula-1-race-weekend-works) where anybody is trying to answer the question the race will ask.

The trouble is that nobody publishes those runs. They have to be reconstructed lap by lap, and this is exactly what we did with the timing data. Every timed lap is matched to the tyre stint it belongs to, a stint being one set of tyres from fitting to removal. The out-lap and the in-lap go straight in the bin, because the lap leaving the pits is always slow and the last lap of a stint is the driver already backing off to come in. Neither is race pace.

A stint only counts at all if eight or more timed laps are left after that. Five laps is a qualifying simulation with the fuel taken out, and a race run needs length. Inside each run we then reject any lap more than seven per cent slower than that run's own fastest, which at Monza means a lap spent behind somebody, and traffic is not tyre wear. What survives is reported as a median rather than an average, because one ruined lap drags an average by several tenths and moves a median by nothing.

The degradation column is the same idea applied to time: the median of the last third of the run minus the median of the first third. A positive number means the driver slowed down as the tyre went off. A negative one means the run got quicker, which on a Friday usually means the track was rubbering in and the fuel was burning off faster than the tyre was wearing out.

Two things this cannot do, stated up front. It cannot see fuel loads, because nobody outside the garage can, and teams deliberately run different amounts. And it is a filter, so it throws out real running: [Oliver Bearman](/drivers/oliver-bearman) put ten timed laps on a set of mediums in this session and only seven of them came through clean, one short of the three-quarters bar, so the [Haas](/teams/haas) is missing from the table below.

![Oliver Bearman's Haas on track at Monza](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Oliver_Bearman_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg/1280px-Oliver_Bearman_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg)

*Bearman at Monza in 2025, a year before the ten-lap run that this analysis threw out. Eustace Bagge, [CC BY 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Oliver_Bearman_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_qualifying.jpg), via Wikimedia Commons.*

It can also let the wrong thing in. [Gabriel Bortoleto](/drivers/gabriel-bortoleto) heads the same table computed for [Friday morning](/series/f1/weekend/13/practice-1), with a soft-tyre median of 1:25.671, and he should not, because that stint contains a 1:24.006 and two laps slower than 1:29.9. It is not a race run, it is a race run with a qualifying lap buried in the middle of it, and because the seven per cent gate is measured from the fastest lap in the run, one very quick lap holds the gate open. We are showing you the FP2 table for that reason. The morning session is dirtier.

## The Monza race runs, second practice

| Pos | Driver | Team | Tyre | Laps | Median | Deg |
|---:|---|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| 1 | [Kimi Antonelli](/drivers/kimi-antonelli) | [Mercedes](/teams/mercedes) | Hard | 17 | 1:26.018 | +0.085 |
| 2 | [Liam Lawson](/drivers/liam-lawson) | [Red Bull](/teams/red-bull-racing) | Hard | 14 | 1:26.046 | +0.225 |
| 3 | [George Russell](/drivers/george-russell) | [Mercedes](/teams/mercedes) | Hard | 10 | 1:26.148 | -0.146 |
| 4 | [Charles Leclerc](/drivers/charles-leclerc) | [Ferrari](/teams/ferrari) | Soft | 12 | 1:26.168 | -0.095 |
| 5 | [Lewis Hamilton](/drivers/lewis-hamilton) | [Ferrari](/teams/ferrari) | Soft | 11 | 1:26.261 | -0.170 |
| 6 | [Liam Lawson](/drivers/liam-lawson) | [Red Bull](/teams/red-bull-racing) | Soft | 10 | 1:26.730 | -0.648 |
| 7 | [Arvid Lindblad](/drivers/arvid-lindblad) | [Racing Bulls](/teams/racing-bulls) | Medium | 10 | 1:26.974 | -0.496 |
| 8 | [Pierre Gasly](/drivers/pierre-gasly) | [Alpine](/teams/alpine) | Hard | 10 | 1:27.072 | -0.294 |
| 9 | [Carlos Sainz](/drivers/carlos-sainz) | [Williams](/teams/williams) | Soft | 12 | 1:27.395 | -0.064 |
| 10 | Yuki Tsunoda | [Racing Bulls](/teams/racing-bulls) | Medium | 12 | 1:27.403 | -0.173 |
| 11 | [Alexander Albon](/drivers/alexander-albon) | [Williams](/teams/williams) | Medium | 10 | 1:27.703 | -0.173 |
| 12 | [Esteban Ocon](/drivers/esteban-ocon) | [Haas](/teams/haas) | Soft | 10 | 1:27.736 | +0.424 |
| 13 | [Nico Hulkenberg](/drivers/nico-hulkenberg) | [Audi](/teams/audi) | Soft | 8 | 1:27.766 | -0.342 |
| 14 | [Valtteri Bottas](/drivers/valtteri-bottas) | [Cadillac](/teams/cadillac) | Soft | 11 | 1:28.225 | +0.531 |
| 15 | [Sergio Perez](/drivers/sergio-perez) | [Cadillac](/teams/cadillac) | Soft | 11 | 1:28.677 | +1.292 |
| 16 | [Lance Stroll](/drivers/lance-stroll) | [Aston Martin](/teams/aston-martin) | Soft | 9 | 1:30.281 | -1.535 |

Laps is the number of timed laps in the run. The median is taken from the ones that survived the traffic filter, which is 17 of 17 for Antonelli, 12 of 14 for Lawson and 9 of 12 for Leclerc. Lawson appears twice because he did two long runs, which nobody else managed.

## The fastest man on Friday started nineteenth

[Antonelli](/drivers/kimi-antonelli) ran seventeen timed laps on the hard tyre, close to a third of a race distance and the longest run anybody put together all afternoon. His last five laps of it were 0.085s slower than his first five. Over a stint that long that is flat, and nobody else in the session went past fourteen laps, so the tyre under him at the end of it was older than anything else out there.

Two days later he won the [Italian Grand Prix](/series/f1/weekend/13/race) from nineteenth on the grid, having taken a full new power unit by choice.

[Russell](/drivers/george-russell) was third quickest on race pace and finished second. [Arvid Lindblad](/drivers/arvid-lindblad) was seventh and finished eighth. [Esteban Ocon](/drivers/esteban-ocon) was twelfth here and, measured against the same set of drivers, finished in exactly the position this table put him.

Take the thirteen drivers who both set a measurable race run and finished the race. Rank them against each other on Friday's pace, then rank them against each other on Sunday's result. Eleven of the thirteen are within two places of themselves, and eight are within one.

The two that miss are worth naming, because both have reasons. [Lawson](/drivers/liam-lawson) had the second-best race pace of the session and finished fourteenth, having started from the pit lane, which is not a fair test of anything. [Nico Hulkenberg](/drivers/nico-hulkenberg) went the other way, thirteenth on this table and twelfth in the race, which sounds like one place and is four once you take out the drivers who never set a measurable run.

## The caveat you have to apply before believing any of it

The top three runs are all on the hard tyre, so they can be compared straight across. Places four and five cannot. [Leclerc](/drivers/charles-leclerc) and [Lewis Hamilton](/drivers/lewis-hamilton) did their running on softs, which is the quickest tyre in the range and the least durable, so a soft-shod median flatters the car that set it. Reading a table like this across compounds is the classic mistake, and [Ferrari](/teams/ferrari) sitting fourth and fifth on softs is exactly where it would bite.

There is a warning about it inside the data. Lawson ran both compounds at length, the only driver who did. His soft run came first, laps 10 to 21, at 1:26.730. His hard run came later, laps 22 to 37, at 1:26.046, which is 0.684s quicker on the harder tyre. That is not the compound talking. It is fuel coming out of the car and rubber going down on the track, and if those two effects can swamp a compound difference over the same afternoon in the same [Red Bull](/teams/red-bull-racing), they can swamp the gaps between neighbouring rows of this table as well.

Treat the top three as a genuine comparison. Treat everything else as a rough sort.

## And there is a hole where the podium was

Here is the part that has to be said out loud rather than tucked into a footnote. [McLaren](/teams/mclaren) and [Max Verstappen](/drivers/max-verstappen) did no race running in second practice at all.

[Lando Norris](/drivers/lando-norris)' longest stint of the afternoon was six timed laps. [Oscar Piastri](/drivers/oscar-piastri)'s was five, and Verstappen's was five. None of the three reaches the eight-lap bar, so none of them is in the table, and the morning does not rescue it either: Verstappen was not entered in [first practice](/series/f1/weekend/13/practice-1), with Ayumu Iwasa in his car for the rookie session, and Norris' longest stint of that session was seven laps. Piastri is the only one of the three with a qualifying long run anywhere on Friday, and it is a morning one, eight laps on mediums at 1:26.704.

They finished third, fourth and fifth.

So the analysis has a hole in it precisely where most of the podium ended up, and anybody who tells you Friday long runs predicted this race is not looking at what is missing. The data describes the cars that ran. It cannot describe the ones that did not.

## Gasly, and the two Fridays

![Franco Colapinto's Alpine on track at Monza](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Franco_Colapinto_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_FP3.jpg/1280px-Franco_Colapinto_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_FP3.jpg)

*Colapinto in the Alpine at Monza in 2025. Eustace Bagge, [CC BY 4.0](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Franco_Colapinto_2025_Italian_Grand_Prix_FP3.jpg), via Wikimedia Commons.*

[Gasly](/drivers/pierre-gasly) is the whole argument in one driver. On the classification he was fourteenth, and on Saturday he was on pole, so the sheet everybody reads got the biggest story of the weekend completely wrong.

On race pace he was eighth of sixteen, in a low-drag [Alpine](/teams/alpine) on hards at 1:27.072. He finished seventh. His pole never suggested seventh. His long run did, two days before the race and before anybody knew there was anything to suggest.

His team-mate never produced a number you can put beside his. [Franco Colapinto](/drivers/franco-colapinto) is absent from the table because his afternoon came in short stints, and his one long run of the weekend was ten laps on mediums in the morning, at 1:27.091. That is a different session on a different compound, so setting it next to Gasly's is precisely the comparison this piece has just told you not to make. He finished ninth, one place behind his team-mate.

Gasly was not in the car in the morning at all, with Paul Aron taking the Alpine for the rookie session. One hard-tyre stint on Friday afternoon is therefore the entire long-run record of the team that started the race from pole.

## What Friday was actually worth

Our view: the race runs did not predict this Grand Prix, and it is worth being precise about what they did instead. Sunday at Monza was decided by a red flag, a [Ferrari](/teams/ferrari) collision on the first lap, a crash at the Parabolica on the second, and a grid full of penalties. No timing data anywhere forecasts that. What the long runs described was the order the cars would settle into once all of it had been spent, and on that they were close to right, which is a more useful thing than a prediction.

The practical version is simpler. If you watch Friday afternoon for the classification, you are watching an entertainment product. The information is in the stints, it is free, and it takes an hour with a spreadsheet to pull out. It is the only part of the weekend where a car in the state it will race in gets to run for long enough to tell you anything, and the sport barely mentions it.

We would rather have three more long runs from the front-running teams than the whole of the qualifying simulation. This weekend the three cars we most wanted them from produced nothing usable at all, and there is a lesson in that too: the teams with the best cars have the least to gain from showing you.

## Where it leaves us

**For the books:** Antonelli's seventeen timed laps on the hard were the longest race run of second practice and the quickest, at a median of 1:26.018 with 0.085s between the start of it and the end; the fastest race pace on Friday belonged to the man who started the Grand Prix nineteenth and won it; eleven of the thirteen drivers who set a measurable run and finished the race ended within two places of where Friday ranked them; Gasly was eighth of sixteen on race pace and seventh on Sunday, from pole; and McLaren's longest stint of the session was six laps against Verstappen's five, from cars that finished third, fourth and fifth.

The sessions themselves are on the [Practice 1](/series/f1/weekend/13/practice-1), [Practice 2](/series/f1/weekend/13/practice-2) and [Practice 3](/series/f1/weekend/13/practice-3) pages, Saturday is on the [Qualifying page](/series/f1/weekend/13/qualifying), Sunday is on the [race page](/series/f1/weekend/13/race), the whole thing including the declared upgrades is on the [Italian Grand Prix hub](/series/f1/weekend/13), and the running totals are on the [standings](/series/f1/standings). The lap and stint data all of this is built from comes from [OpenF1](https://openf1.org/), which publishes it openly.

Monza is the circuit where the low-fuel lap is least honest, because a tow is worth more here than anywhere. It is also, for the same reason, the circuit where the long run is worth most. Friday told us which car would be quickest over a stint on Sunday. It just did not tell the people who were reading the other number.
